title: Digital Age ~ CLO6 Launch Event Replay [Continuously Updated] p03 H&M Speech
description: Missed the live broadcast? No time to watch it live? No worries! The CLO6 launch event replay is here~ Come and check it out!
transcript:
Hello everyone, the topic I would like to share with you today is 3D virtual technology, how to be creative and sustainable.  
First of all, I would like to apologize because today's presentation is in English. I was too busy with work and didn't have time to translate it into Chinese. But I will try my best to make it clear, and I will have time to answer questions at the end.  

First of all, let me introduce myself. My name is Wang Chen, also known as Clara. I graduated from the Department of Fashion Design at the University of London. I also studied fashion and finance with a French teacher for a period of time, so I was born with a background in design.  

In 2017, as a 3D designer, I joined the H&M Creative Lab and worked with all H&M brands and categories. I studied and worked there until I became a senior. Today, as a business expert, I joined the company's business tech. Now I am mainly responsible for everything related to 3D. We hope to use my previous experience to accelerate the digital transformation and the use of new technologies in the company.  

Let me briefly introduce H&M, because I guess not everyone knows us very well. We have been in Sweden since 1947. We started our first H&M store in the city of Västerås. H&M Group has been a global fashion enthusiast for 73 years. We are a brand family. Apart from H&M, we also have COS, & Other Stories, ARKET, MONKI, WEEKDAY, H&M HOME, and ARKET. Apart from WEEKDAY and ARKET, we can buy everything else in China. We hope to provide fashion design and service to our customers in an exciting and sustainable way.  

We want to bring inspiration and personal style to our customers. With the rapid change in fashion sales and the COVID-19 pandemic, we have accelerated the development of digital and integrated channels. We have improved our work methods and become more flexible, fast, and efficient. All of this is to meet the constant needs of our customers.  

As our customers' expectations continue to increase, it means that we need to work more passionately. Our goal is to provide the best combination of fashion, quality, price, and sustainability.  

I would like to focus on the sustainable development vision of our group. We want to be a fair and equal enterprise, leading the change in fashion towards circularity and climate positivity. Our sustainable development work covers the entire value chain. We focus not only on our own operations but also on the interests of other stakeholders and the entire industry.  

Our global sustainable development team has a total of 270 employees. It is one of the largest sustainable development organizations in this industry and others. We believe that we need enough people and power to promote this sustainable development work and lead the change in the industry.  

In fact, from the very beginning, the mission of H&M Group was to democratize fashion. Today, this means that it is sustainable. This is the only way we can provide fashion and design to all our customers.  

Based on our vision, the three key areas of our sustainable development strategy are 100% circular and climate positive, 100% fairness and equality, and 100% leadership in change. In the future, I believe that the future of H&M Group will be much brighter.  

Now we will move on to the next part of the H&M Group's vision, which is the H&M industry's digital technology. This is actually an important part of sustainable development.  

As you can see in the background, this is our first attempt three years ago. This is a milestone of our product integration technology. As you can see, we started from fabric simulation. From 2014 to 2017, we mainly simulated wool, silk, and lace fabrics. The 2D simulation here is actually different from the ordinary 2D surface. The fabric we simulate also produces a technical package directly, which is a tech pack, which can be produced directly at the factory. So this is a technical plus design step. At the same time, the professional knowledge of this team of designers actually has higher requirements.  

After having the fabric, in 2017, we started to try 3D fabric. We started from 3D knitted fabric to 3D shrink fabric, 3D wool fabric, 3D socks and hats, and then we went on to wool clothes, underwear, and so on. Then we expanded to more and more different types. As we expanded, we introduced new talents, technology, and equipment.  

So in this picture, actually, we included at least four to five software and equipment. You might ask, what did we try in 2019 to 2020? But I can't share this with you today.  

Regarding avatars, I believe everyone here is a user, so everyone knows that avatar refers to the platform in our reality. So after the clothing industry started to use 3D technology, the necessary elements in reality needed to be digitized. This is our so-called digital twin. Ideally, we certainly hope that the digital world can truly simulate the real world, and even predict the real world. So the correct size of the avatar is actually very important, because with it, you can do real, effective 3D simulation in the business.  

Next, I will introduce a few applications under different scenarios. First of all, this is a T-shirt of a girl from H&M and a shirt of a boy. Through this 3D virtual technology, we can try and display different colors, patterns, and prints without any physical samples. And then during the design process, we can boldly try different proportions and combinations.  

So in fact, if the designer might have had to print it out in the past, put it on the sample, and compare it, it might be wrong and then print it again. So this kind of long process can now be done directly in the 3D system. And then for the designers who are very familiar with the style, basically they can make the decision to order directly.  

This is the next talk I will be conducting. Because it is online, can they hear your voice? Is it because of your PPT? Yes, it is. It helps me.  

And then the next one is, this is a demonstration of the same style, the same pattern, and the different seam lines, the different bases. Of course, we also first simulated the 2D fabric, and then simulated the 3D layer. In fact, as long as the rendering is clear enough, the buyer and the designer can also make the decision directly. So this is a demonstration of the 3D full print of COSKITS, the print of the print, and the display of the 3D full pattern of COSKITS.  

Of course, first of all, you need to have the full pattern of this avatar to be realized. And then, we currently only recommend using it to see the overall proportion of the clothes and the proportion of the print, including the position on the clothes. Because you may find that some designs look good with small patterns, and after enlarging, you may not be able to see them. So, you may not be able to see them. But at the moment, we actually found that there may still be some limitations when it comes to the fitting of the 3D set.  

And then this is a series of our exhibitions. What this picture shows is our brand, MONKI, in 2018, a bag series. This is also the first brand of H&M Group to try to simulate the whole series with 3D. And then on the picture, it simply shows some of our cooperation at the time.  

You may know that this collection line-up is usually made up exactly of 2D sketches or photos. Normally, the process is not that intuitive. It's only possible to have the sample image in the photo. So, the whole series can be clearly displayed in 3D at an early stage, and this is the concept of the collection, and also the colors, and the pattern ratio, saving us a lot of sample time.  

In fact, a lot of our online buyers saw the whole 3D series, and basically took all the orders.  

Similarly, this is Other Stories AOA Team’s bold attempt. They did everything from design, sampling, to fitting all based on 3D simulation, fast design, fast decision-making. For simpler styles, we directly simulated the fitting in 3D; for more complex styles, we used VSR for fitting. So this entire series only required one round of 15 samples.  

To add, all of this was completed remotely, so there was inevitably coordination and communication with the merchandisers at the same time.  

3D virtual technology also has a very big advantage: it can accumulate digital assets. Once a piece of clothing is built, it can be shared and reused. For the next season, you only need to simply modify or change colors and prints. As your digital assets accumulate, your efficiency will increase, and the reduction in physical sampling is very environmentally friendly.  

Overall, the benefits of 3D virtual technology are very obvious. Previously, people could see that from an idea until the final product that customers can buy, there would be many samples involved. From prototype to development to quotation to size set to communication to counter sample, and finally production sample.  

What we want to emphasize is that we hope 3D virtual technology reduces the number of physical samples from prototype to size-set samples. Here, we say reduce, not replace.  

In the early stages, these benefits are clear, especially from the design perspective, it is truly a disruptive design process. During development, it also clearly shortens our development time, increases accuracy, and saves a lot of physical samples. In communication, it is very direct; it is a visual communication, so it reduces many misunderstandings and speeds up decision-making.  

Of course, from a sustainability standpoint, it is very environmentally friendly because you don’t need to produce a lot of physical samples.  

But at the same time, 3D virtual technology also has its limitations. We found that you can use 3D to make a story decision for colors, i.e., decide what colors you want to do this year. But everyone knows that different colors show differently on different materials. So when you decide on the color you want to order this year, as to what exact shade of red or blue it is, you still need to produce physical color samples. So this step cannot be omitted.  

Including complex materials like sequins and pleats, we found that if you want to achieve exactly the same effect in 3D, the time spent in 3D is far more than the supplier’s direct feedback time for 15 samples. So based on this, we still decide to produce 15 physical samples for some more complex materials. This is a balancing process.  

Regarding underwear, so far we only use 3D for aesthetic decisions; we cannot yet do any technical fitting. This is the transformation we are working on.  

Everyone knows that the fashion industry has not changed much in over 100 years, but what is most obvious now is that our tools are starting to change. Previously, you could see dress forms, our draping systems, and physical fabrics. Now our tools are gradually becoming virtual dress forms. Our patterns may be created by new software that directly interfaces with 3D software for pattern making. Our fabrics are also designed virtually and then produced.  

It is important to emphasize that 3D virtual samples do not exist independently, so it’s not that the more beautiful your 3D is, the better. What we call a "good" 3D virtual sample must be validated with physical samples. Without validation, 3D is not reliable enough to make decisions. So 3D and physical samples are not a replacement process; they are interdependent.  

Finally, I will share some of the lessons we have learned, which can be simply summarized as follows:  

The prerequisite for 3D virtual technology includes hardware, software, and the industry-related knowledge and experience—you must understand these.  

Secondly, the process—you need to understand the balance between the time spent and the result you want to achieve, and how best to embed this into your existing processes.  

Thirdly, people—people are extremely critical. For new technology, you must find ways to build trust because many new tech initiatives initially face setbacks. Building trust is very important. Then comes adoption, adaptation, and possibly new functional shifts in work.  

It still requires involvement; it is not just a standalone software. You can’t say your digital transformation is done with one 3D software. It requires people, products, and many aspects working together as a team to push it forward.  

Finally, you must have a central and clear architecture to manage all your 3D assets, including storage systems, tracking systems, and these still require a lot of time and manpower. So digital transformation truly requires a full-time team to work on it.  

That’s all for my sharing today. Thank you all. Our team members Sovia, Cloris, and Sijia are here on site, and you can talk to them later. If anyone has questions for Clara, please raise your hand to ask.  

Thank you for your sharing.  

Question: On H&M’s official website, do you use 3D images on some detail pages, or do you use physical photos?  

Answer: That’s company confidential, so I can’t tell you. But I can share that, for example, you know that brands like Uniqlo use all CG images on their website—they are all simulations.  

Question: The pattern you’re creating, are you using additional structured pattern software, or are you using another 2D software for pattern making?  

Answer: Actually, our pattern makers create patterns in Lectra and then import them into CLO. So currently, they don’t create directly in CLO.  

Question: How do you transfer changes made in 3D to physical samples?  

Answer: That’s a very good question. If you want to change your product through your design process, we have also trained our merchandisers. So we need our merchandisers to make changes in 3D along with our design team.  

Thank you.  

Another question?  

Question: I want to ask, which are the main dialog companies we know? What is the efficiency of how many pieces they can make? Do you monitor that kind of report? What is the efficiency of one supplier in creating a sample?  

Answer: The efficiency really depends on the complexity or the familiarity of our supplier. We have different levels of suppliers.  

Question: Do you level them? Because in production, we compare all those efficiencies. Because this is digital sampling, right? So maybe comparing the same product complexity, do you think about it or plan to do something in that direction?  

Answer: We are on our way to it. We are trying to build a system to help us evaluate. So I can just say we are on our way.  

Thank you. Thank you so much.  

Welcome. Great presentation.  

Clara, sorry, I have another question. Because we are also doing this.  

It’s okay, you are the first. Thank you. I really understand.  

I want to ask, in the whole supply chain, how many years do you expect it to last? How many years do you think it will take to use this product in the industry? How do you standardize it? How do you standardize the production process and communication process?  

Answer: We do have a vision, but I can’t say it now. To be honest, this estimate—I can’t say our estimate is accurate. But we do have a timeline. We have a vision. We hope to lead to—for example, by the end of this year, we hope we can... Just like our sustainability, we also have a very clear vision. For example, by 2023, we hope all our fabrics will be environmentally friendly. Yes, we have a vision, but I can’t say it now.  

Thank you.  

Actually, my question is related to the previous question because she asked about the fabric. I just want to ask about the development phase. H&M is now in the development phase using this. How much do you want to reduce the amount of physical samples?  

Answer: As you just saw, reducing the number of physical samples is not a goal; it is a side effect. Especially when you try new software, H&M is such a big company that it is very careful. So far, we are just calculating. We hope it can reduce physical samples as much as possible. It’s not that our goal is to reduce physical samples, but as you saw, we have a lot of sample runs. We hope we can remove at least one to two sample runs. Like this.  

Yes.  

Thank you.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to 3D Virtual Technology in Fashion at H&M This section introduces Wang Chen (Clara), a senior 3D designer and business expert at H&M Creative Lab, and outlines H&M Group’s background, brand family, and commitment to digital transformation and sustainability in fashion. Wang Chen graduated from the University of London in Fashion Design and has experience in both design and finance. She joined H&M Creative Lab in 2017 as a 3D designer and now leads 3D-related digital transformation efforts within the company’s business technology division. H&M Group, founded in Sweden in 1947, includes multiple brands such as COS, & Other Stories, ARKET, MONKI, WEEKDAY, and H&M HOME. Except for WEEKDAY and ARKET, all are available in China. H&M focuses on providing fashion that is inspiring, personal, and sustainable while adapting to rapidly changing fashion sales channels and customer expectations, especially accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The group’s sustainability vision emphasizes fairness, equality, circularity, and climate positivity across the entire value chain, supported by a global team of 270 employees. The mission to democratize fashion now integrates sustainability as a core principle, aiming for 100% circularity, climate positivity, fairness, equality, and leadership in industry change. --- ## H&M’s Digital Technology Vision and 3D Virtual Technology Evolution This section covers H&M’s integration of digital technology into their sustainable development strategy, focusing on 3D virtual technology for fabric simulation, digital twins, and product development. H&M began fabric simulation around 2014, focusing initially on wool, silk, and lace fabrics using advanced 2D simulation that generates technical packages (“tech packs”) directly producible by factories, combining design and technical specifications. By 2017, H&M expanded into 3D fabric simulation, covering knitted fabrics, shrink fabrics, wool, socks, hats, underwear, and more. This development involved multiple software platforms and specialized equipment, reflecting continuous technology and talent acquisition. “Digital twins” represent virtual avatars that simulate real-world human forms with precise sizing. These avatars are critical for realistic 3D garment simulation, enabling effective virtual fitting and design validation. --- ## Applications of 3D Virtual Technology in Design and Sampling This section explains practical applications of 3D virtual technology in H&M’s design and sampling processes, highlighting efficiencies gained and current limitations. 3D technology allows designers to try different colors, patterns, proportions, and combinations virtually without producing physical samples. This accelerates design decisions, reduces errors, and enables immediate visualization of designs. Examples include: - Virtual try-ons of T-shirts and shirts with various colors and prints. - 3D full print demonstrations for COSKITS, showing different seam lines and fabric bases. - MONKI’s 2018 bag series, which was the first full collection simulated entirely in 3D, allowing early visualization of colors, patterns, and concepts, significantly reducing sample time. - Other Stories AOA Team’s collection, designed, sampled, and fitted almost entirely via 3D, requiring only one round of 15 physical samples, even when done remotely. 3D virtual assets are reusable and modifiable for future seasons, increasing efficiency and reducing environmental impact by minimizing physical samples.

chunks.title: Digital Age ~ CLO6 Launch Event Replay [Continuously Updated] p03 H&M Speech
chunks.content: - 3D full print demonstrations for COSKITS, showing different seam lines and fabric bases. - MONKI’s 2018 bag series, which was the first full collection simulated entirely in 3D, allowing early visualization of colors, patterns, and concepts, significantly reducing sample time. - Other Stories AOA Team’s collection, designed, sampled, and fitted almost entirely via 3D, requiring only one round of 15 physical samples, even when done remotely. 3D virtual assets are reusable and modifiable for future seasons, increasing efficiency and reducing environmental impact by minimizing physical samples. --- ## Benefits and Limitations of 3D Virtual Technology in Fashion This section discusses the benefits of 3D virtual technology along with its current limitations in the fashion industry. ### Benefits: - Significant reduction in physical samples needed from prototype to size-set stages (though not full replacement). - Disruptive improvements in design processes, development speed, and accuracy. - Enhanced visual communication between teams, reducing misunderstandings and speeding decision-making. - Environmental sustainability through fewer physical samples. - Digital asset accumulation for reuse and modification. ### Limitations: - Precise color matching remains challenging; physical color samples are still required to confirm exact shades on materials. - Complex materials such as sequins and pleats require extensive 3D simulation time, often exceeding the time suppliers take to produce physical samples, so physical sampling remains necessary. - For underwear, 3D is currently used only for aesthetic decisions, with technical fitting still relying on physical methods. - 3D virtual samples must be validated against physical samples; they are interdependent, not replacements. --- ## Transformations in Fashion Industry Tools and Processes This section outlines how 3D virtual technology is transforming traditional fashion tools and workflows. Traditional tools like dress forms, draping systems, and physical fabrics are increasingly being replaced by virtual equivalents. Pattern creation is evolving with software that interfaces directly with 3D applications (e.g., Lectra patterns imported into CLO 3D). However, a good 3D virtual sample depends on validation with physical samples, reinforcing a hybrid workflow integrating both virtual and physical stages. --- ## Key Lessons and Prerequisites for Implementing 3D Virtual Technology This section summarizes important lessons learned by H&M in adopting 3D virtual technology, emphasizing prerequisites and organizational factors. ### Prerequisites: - Hardware, software, and deep industry knowledge and experience are essential. - Understanding the balance between time investment and desired results is crucial. - Integration of 3D into existing workflows must be thoughtful and strategic. ### People and Adoption: - Building trust in new technology is critical, as initial setbacks are common. - Adoption involves adaptation and may shift functional roles. - Digital transformation is not about standalone software but requires coordinated teamwork across people, products, and processes. ### Infrastructure and Management: - A centralized architecture is necessary to manage 3D assets, including storage and tracking systems. - Digital transformation requires dedicated full-time teams for maintenance and advancement. --- ## Audience Q&A Highlights This section captures key questions and responses related to H&M’s 3D virtual technology practices and future plans.

chunks.content: - Adoption involves adaptation and may shift functional roles. - Digital transformation is not about standalone software but requires coordinated teamwork across people, products, and processes. ### Infrastructure and Management: - A centralized architecture is necessary to manage 3D assets, including storage and tracking systems. - Digital transformation requires dedicated full-time teams for maintenance and advancement. --- ## Audience Q&A Highlights This section captures key questions and responses related to H&M’s 3D virtual technology practices and future plans. - **Use of 3D images on official website:** Company confidential. Comparable brands like Uniqlo use fully CG-simulated images online. - **Pattern software:** Patterns are created in Lectra and imported into CLO; direct pattern creation in CLO is not currently done. - **Transferring 3D changes to physical samples:** Merchandisers are trained to implement changes in 3D alongside the design team for consistency. - **Supplier efficiency:** Varies by supplier expertise and product complexity; H&M is developing systems to evaluate and monitor sample production efficiency. - **Industry adoption timeline and standardization:** H&M has a vision and timeline but does not disclose specific estimates. They aim for sustainability goals, such as all fabrics being environmentally friendly by 2023. - **Physical sample reduction goals:** Reducing physical samples is a beneficial side effect rather than a primary goal. The company seeks to remove at least one to two sample runs, proceeding carefully due to company scale and complexity. --- # Summary This document presents a detailed overview of H&M’s integration of 3D virtual technology as part of their sustainable development and digital transformation strategy. It discusses the evolution of fabric simulation, avatar development, and practical applications in design and sampling, highlighting both benefits and current limitations. The transformation of traditional fashion tools, key lessons in implementation, and audience insights provide a comprehensive understanding of how 3D virtual technology is reshaping the fashion industry at H&M.
